answer.rationale: Only memory_c2 speaks directly to the one lever that can satisfy an 18% mandate the incumbent has refused to negotiate (memory_c4's renegotiation path is closed this cycle; memory_c6's multi-year discount and memory_c5's deferral do not clear the mandate and deferral is impossible with a 14-day hard expiry). So memory_c2 is the load-bearing memory and the only one worth my single verification pull. What I need from the archive is what memory_c2 does not say: it attests to unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy \u2014 back-office and price signals \u2014 but says nothing about on-time delivery performance at or near committed volume. That is precisely the dimension that matters at 94% utilization with no buffer, and a favorable cost record can be silently carried forward as a general reliability endorsement it never earned. It is also a single prior-year observation that, unlike memory_c3's second source, was never stress-tested through a shortage. Intent: move primary supply to the low-cost vendor, but as a guarded staged ramp \u2014 qualify on a bounded volume slice with the incumbent bridged on short-term terms, with explicit on-time-delivery gates before each volume step. This spends the single decision on the only mandate-clearing option while refusing to convert a cost-and-invoicing record into an unhedged bet on delivery. If the archive shows memory_c2's volumes were far below current committed volume, the ramp gates tighten and I would rather miss the mandate this cycle than break the line; if it shows delivery was measured at comparable volume, the ramp accelerates. Residual uncertainty stays live either way, and I am not treating the cost quote as evidence of capacity.
